title: The Great Indian Spice Race: How Diaspora Brands and Legacy Giants Are Battling for America's Kitchen
excerpt: From MDH's $3.99 bags at Patel Brothers to Diaspora Co.'s $12 single-origin turmeric on Instagram — the fight over who owns Indian flavour in America is heating up.
body:
Behind every great Indian grocery run in America, there is a quiet transformation happening on the shelves. Where once the spice aisle was dominated by generic packets of turmeric and chilli powder from commodity traders, a new generation of Indian spice brands is rewriting the rules — paying farmers more, delivering fresher product, and turning the humble masala dabba into a premium consumer category.

The US herbs and spices market reached $10.53 billion in 2024, and Indian spices are at the centre of its fastest-growing segment. Import values of crushed and ground chili peppers from India have surged from $52.5 million to $86.5 million between 2019 and 2023, a 65 percent increase. But behind these numbers is a more interesting story: the battle between legacy Indian spice giants and a wave of direct-to-consumer disruptors fighting over who gets to define "authentic" for the American kitchen.

## The Legacy Giants Expand

MDH and Everest, the twin pillars of every Indian household's spice shelf, have long dominated America's Indian grocery stores. Founded in 1919 and 1967 respectively, these brands built their reputations on affordability and consistency — the Garam Masala your grandmother used is the same Garam Masala you will find at Patel Brothers in Edison or Devon Avenue in Chicago.

But the US market for these brands has traditionally been limited to ethnic grocery stores catering to Indian shoppers. The opportunity now is whether they can cross over into mainstream American retail, where turmeric lattes, chai concentrates, and curry kits have already primed consumers for Indian flavours without necessarily knowing the brands behind them.

## The Disruptors

Diaspora Co., founded by Sana Javeri Kadri, has become the poster child of a different approach. The Oakland-based company sources single-origin spices directly from small family farms across India and Sri Lanka, paying farmers an average of three to five times the commodity price. By the end of 2025, the brand planned to be on 1,000 grocery store shelves.

The pitch is not just quality — it is story. Each Diaspora Co. spice comes with the name of the farm, the region, and the harvest date. Their Aranya Black Pepper from Kerala has been described by the Los Angeles Times as "an epiphany." It is the kind of provenance narrative that resonates with the same American consumers who pay $18 for single-origin coffee beans.

Meanwhile, From Byadgi has entered the market with a laser focus on a single product: Byadgi chilli powder from Karnataka's legendary Byadgi region. The GI-certified chilli is prized for its deep natural red colour, mild heat, and sweet pepper notes. In a market where most American consumers cannot distinguish between chilli powders, the brand is betting that specificity — not breadth — is the way to stand out.

## Why This Matters for NRIs

For Indian Americans, the spice aisle has always been a site of identity. The brands you buy say something about who you are: the NRI who shops exclusively at the Indian grocery store, buying 500-gram bags of MDH Chana Masala for $3.99; or the second-generation Indian American who discovers Diaspora Co. through Instagram and pays $12 for a jar of turmeric that comes with a farmer's photograph.

Both are valid. Both serve a real need. But the gap between them — in price, in narrative, in who profits at the farm level — is the central tension of Indian food's American moment. As turmeric, ghee, and chai continue their march into mainstream wellness culture, the question of who benefits from that mainstreaming becomes more urgent.

Ghee offers a telling example. Once dismissed as "clarified butter" in American cookbooks, it is now proudly labelled as ghee on restaurant menus from Washington, D.C. to San Francisco. Brands like Pure Indian Foods, a fifth-generation family business, sell organic grassfed ghee infused with turmeric, ginger, and black pepper — positioned as an Ayurvedic superfood rather than a cooking fat. The product sits comfortably on Whole Foods shelves alongside MCT oils and adaptogenic powders.

## The Supply Chain Revolution

The deeper story is about supply chains. India's spice trade has historically been opaque — farmers sell to auction houses, spices change hands multiple times, and by the time a jar of turmeric reaches an American kitchen, it may be years old and a shadow of what it once was.

Brands like Diaspora Co. and From Byadgi are trying to short-circuit that chain, but they face their own challenges: scaling direct trade while maintaining quality, navigating USDA import regulations, and convincing American consumers that a $12 jar of turmeric is worth five times the commodity alternative.

## What's Next

The convergence of Indian food going mainstream in American restaurants, the wellness industry's embrace of Ayurvedic ingredients, and a generation of Indian American entrepreneurs rethinking the spice trade suggests this is still early innings. The US spice market is projected to continue growing at a robust pace through the end of the decade. For the Indian farmers, brands, and diaspora communities at the centre of this shift, the stakes — and the spice — have never been higher.
